titular: Bitcoin drops below $70,000 and $1.3bn in borrowed-money bets is wiped out
resum: Bitcoin fell below $70,000 in the early hours of Friday, its lowest level since 19 August. Over 24 hours, trading platforms forcibly closed more than $1.3 billion in leveraged contracts, $677 million of them in bitcoin alone, amid the resignation of Nvidia's CEO and five straight days of outflows from bitcoin funds.
per_que_importa: A “liquidation” happens when someone has placed a bet with borrowed money (leverage) and the price moves against them: the platform closes the position and the person loses what they put in. These forced sales can also speed up the fall.

titular: Binance finishes repaying customers the $6.3bn stolen in October's cyberattack
resum: Binance says it has now covered all $6.3 billion in crypto stolen on 29 October, a theft the US attributes to North Korea. It paid using its emergency fund, an insurance fund and its own capital; about $2.8 billion of the stolen funds has been frozen but not yet recovered.
per_que_importa: This time the platform absorbed the loss, but that was the company's choice, not an obligation: in crypto there's no deposit guarantee scheme like the one that protects bank accounts. Customers also had limits on withdrawals for several days.

titular: MSCI will remove Strategy, the big bitcoin buyer, from its stock indices
resum: Index provider MSCI has confirmed that Strategy, the listed company holding the most bitcoin, will leave its indices at the close on 30 November; Japan's Metaplanet and Upexi are being dropped too. JPMorgan had estimated the move could force sales of around $2.8 billion of its shares.
per_que_importa: Many index funds and pension plans track these indices, so they'll stop holding these shares. MSCI considers a company that is mostly a pile of bitcoin to be more like a fund than a business, a reminder that buying its shares is, in effect, a bet on bitcoin.

titular: Deutsche Bank starts holding crypto for large clients in Europe
resum: Germany's biggest bank has launched a service to safekeep and transfer 5 assets for European companies and institutional investors: bitcoin, ether and three stablecoins (USDC, EURC and EURAU). It is licensed under the EU's MiCA rules, but for now it doesn't let clients buy or sell them.
per_que_importa: A big, supervised bank holding crypto doesn't make it any less volatile: the price can rise and fall just the same. What changes is who looks after the keys and which security rules they must follow; and for now, it's a service for large clients, not individuals.

titular: Gemini sells its European and UK business for under $10m
resum: US crypto platform Gemini, run by the Winklevoss twins, has sold its UK and EU subsidiaries to KAST, a stablecoin payments company, for less than $10 million, according to CoinDesk. It had already announced in February that it was pulling out of Europe and cutting 25% of its workforce.
per_que_importa: When a platform changes hands, customer accounts may move to another company with new terms. It's worth checking that the new owner holds a MiCA licence and what happens to account balances.

titular: ABANCA joins the CNMV's crypto register, bringing the total to 7 Spanish banks
resum: Since 6 November, ABANCA has appeared on the list kept by Spain's securities regulator (CNMV) of firms authorised to offer crypto-asset services under the EU's MiCA rules, making it the seventh Spanish bank to do so, according to Criptoinforme. It can hold crypto for customers and pass on their orders, but not execute them directly.
per_que_importa: Your everyday bank offering crypto doesn't make it a safe investment: the risk of losing money is the same. Any gains are taxed under Spanish income tax (IRPF) as capital gains, and the CNMV register lets you check who is authorised.
